articles.title: Why Does My Cat Sleep on Me? What the Habit Can Mean
articles.metaDescription: Learn why cats sleep on people, how warmth, routine and social preference may contribute, and when sudden clinginess or sleep changes deserve veterinary attention.
articles.alt: Relaxed cat sleeping comfortably on its owner
articles.summary: Understand why a cat may choose to sleep on you, how to redirect the habit gently, and why sudden clinginess matters more than the exact sleeping position.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat sleep on me
secondaryKeywords: why does my cat lay on me
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
If your cat regularly settles on your chest, lap, legs, or beside your head, the behavior is usually easier to understand as a combination of comfort, warmth, familiarity, and social preference—not as a single coded message. The useful question is whether this is your cat's normal sleeping habit or a sudden change in how much contact it needs.

What Sleeping on You Can Mean

Your body is warm, carries a familiar scent, and often provides a predictable place to rest. Cats also differ widely in how social they are with people. Some routinely seek body contact; others prefer to stay nearby without touching. Research on cat–human relationships supports the idea that cats can form meaningful social bonds with caregivers, while also showing substantial individual variation.

Warmth and a Stable Resting Surface

A lap, chest, or legs can be warmer than an open bed and may feel physically secure. This is especially attractive in a cool room or during quiet periods when you are not moving much.

Familiarity and Routine

Cats learn household patterns quickly. If you sit in the same chair every evening or lie down at the same time each night, your body may simply be part of a predictable resting routine.

Social Contact

Sleeping close to a person can be one form of voluntary social contact. It does not prove a specific emotion on its own, but it can fit a broader pattern that includes greeting, rubbing, following, relaxed proximity, and choosing to rest nearby.

Why the Exact Sleeping Spot Varies

A cat on your chest may be choosing warmth and a relatively still surface. A cat near your head may prefer the pillow area because it moves less than your legs and carries a strong familiar scent. A cat on your feet may be seeking closeness while keeping an easy exit route. These are reasonable interpretations, not fixed rules.

When the Habit Is Comfortable for the Cat but Not for You

You do not have to sacrifice your own sleep to preserve the relationship. Create an attractive alternative close to where the cat already wants to be. A soft bed or folded blanket beside you is usually easier to teach than a bed across the room.

  1. Place the alternative resting spot close to you at first.
  2. Reward the cat when it chooses that location voluntarily.
  3. Keep bedtime routines predictable.
  4. Move the cat calmly if you need space; avoid startling or punishing it.
  5. Make sure the alternative is easy to reach, especially for senior cats.

Sudden Clinginess Is More Important Than the Sleeping Position

A cat that has slept on you for years and otherwise behaves normally is different from a previously independent cat that suddenly cannot settle unless it is touching you. Household changes can temporarily increase proximity-seeking, but health changes can also alter social behavior.

Watch appetite, weight, thirst, litter-box habits, mobility, grooming, breathing, vocalization, and energy. If the change is new and your cat is also following you constantly, compare the pattern with why cats may suddenly follow their owners more closely. If the change appears mainly after bedtime, nighttime meowing and routine changes may provide additional context.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Sleeping on you by itself is rarely a medical problem. Veterinary advice is appropriate when a major change in sleeping or social behavior appears with weakness, pain, breathing difficulty, reduced appetite, weight loss, increased thirst, confusion, reduced mobility, or another new symptom. The change from your cat's baseline matters more than the exact place it chooses to sleep.

sources.title: My Cat and Me—A Study of Cat Owner Perceptions of Their Bond and Relationship
CATastrophic Myths Part 1: Common Misconceptions About the Social Behavior of Domestic Cats
sources.publisher: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery / PMC

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Knock Things Over? How to Read the Pattern and Reduce It
articles.metaDescription: Learn why cats push objects from tables and shelves, how play and attention can reinforce it, and how to reduce the habit with safer enrichment and setup changes.
articles.alt: Curious cat touching a small safe object on a table
articles.summary: Identify what rewards object-pushing, protect fragile items, provide safer outlets for pawing and play, and know when a sudden behavior change deserves a broader look.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat knock things over
secondaryKeywords: how to stop cat knocking things over
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
A cat that taps a pen, nudges a bottle cap, or pushes a lightweight object from a shelf is usually interacting with movement, novelty, or your response. The behavior can look deliberate because it is deliberate—the cat is moving the object—but that does not mean the goal is to annoy you.

First, Identify What the Cat Gets From the Behavior

Instead of treating every incident as the same problem, watch the sequence. Does the cat keep batting the object after it falls? Does it look at you first? Does it happen near mealtime, while you work at a desk, or only when the house is quiet? The answer helps distinguish object play from attention-seeking or under-stimulation.

The Object Is Interesting to Move

Cats commonly use their paws during play and investigation. Small objects that roll, wobble, slide, or make noise can be more rewarding than a toy that never changes.

Your Reaction May Be Part of the Reward

If every push makes you jump up, talk, chase, or grab the cat, the human response can become part of the event. Even negative attention can make a behavior more predictable and interesting.

The Environment May Need Better Outlets

Indoor cats benefit from opportunities to stalk, chase, pounce, climb, scratch, manipulate objects, and work for food. A cat with few legal activities may create its own.

Change the Setup Before Trying to Correct the Cat

Problem AreaSafer Setup
Desk with pens and small itemsUse drawers or lidded containers and add a nearby perch.
Kitchen counterRemove food residue and keep breakables away from edges.
NightstandStore medication, glasses, batteries, cords, and small electronics safely.
Display shelfMove fragile objects or use secure closed storage.

Environmental management is not a shortcut; it is often the most effective prevention. A cat cannot repeatedly rehearse a behavior with an unsafe item that is no longer available.

Give Pawing and Hunting Behavior a Better Target

Use wand toys, track toys, sturdy balls, food puzzles, and other cat-safe objects that move in interesting ways. Rotate a few toys instead of leaving every toy out all the time. Supervise anything with string, ribbon, feathers, or parts that could be swallowed.

If your cat enjoys manipulating household objects, it may also be attracted to boxes or carried toys. See why boxes can work as feline enrichment and why cats sometimes carry toys to people.

How to Respond in the Moment

If the object is safe, keep your reaction low-key. Avoid yelling, spraying water, or chasing the cat. Reward calm behavior at other times and offer interactive play on a predictable schedule rather than immediately after every crash. If the object is dangerous, intervene for safety and then change the environment so the situation is less likely to repeat.

When a New Increase Deserves a Broader Look

Knocking objects over is usually a behavior problem, not a medical symptom. Still, a sudden major increase in restlessness combined with unusual appetite, thirst, vocalization, sleep, or activity should be considered as a whole. If your cat is also eating much more than usual, review increased appetite in cats and discuss persistent physical changes with a veterinarian.

sources.title: Cat Behavior and Training - Play and Play Toys
Training Techniques for Addressing Undesirable Behaviors
2019 Meeting the Physical and Emotional Needs of Owned Indoor Cats

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Lick Plastic? When Curiosity Becomes a Safety Risk
articles.metaDescription: Learn why cats may lick plastic, how to separate brief curiosity from pica-like behavior, what ingestion risks matter, and when to contact a veterinarian.
articles.alt: Cat sniffing a clean plastic bag while an owner keeps it out of reach
articles.summary: Separate harmless investigation from repeated plastic chewing or ingestion, reduce household hazards, and know when pica-like behavior or obstruction signs require veterinary care.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat lick plastic
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
A cat may lick a plastic bag because it smells like food, feels unusual on the tongue, crinkles when touched, or has become part of a repeated routine. The safety issue begins when licking progresses to chewing or swallowing. Plastic is not a safe toy or chew material.

Separate Brief Investigation From Pica-Like Behavior

A cat that briefly sniffs or licks a grocery bag is different from a cat that repeatedly searches for plastic, bites pieces off, or ingests non-food items. Persistent ingestion of non-food material is described as pica and can have behavioral or medical contributors. It deserves veterinary discussion rather than being dismissed as a quirky preference.

Why Plastic May Attract a Cat

Food packaging can retain odors even when it looks clean. Thin plastic also moves, changes shape, and makes sound when touched, which can make it interesting to investigate. Some cats repeat the behavior because access is easy or because the resulting human reaction becomes predictable.

These explanations are possibilities, not a diagnosis. If the behavior is frequent, escalating, or includes actual swallowing, the priority shifts from interpreting motive to preventing ingestion and looking for contributing health or behavior problems.

Plastic Risks Owners Should Take Seriously

  • Swallowed fragments: non-digestible material can contribute to gastrointestinal obstruction.
  • Long strips or string-like plastic: linear foreign material can be especially dangerous if it becomes anchored and damages the intestine.
  • Bag handles: loops create an entanglement hazard.
  • Tape and adhesive: sticky material can attach to fur or be chewed and swallowed.
  • Food residue: packaging may contain grease, seasonings, or other substances that are not appropriate for cats.

Make Access Difficult and Safe Alternatives Easy

Store shopping bags, packing film, wrappers, tape, rubber bands, and trash inside closed cabinets or secure bins. Do not leave plastic bags out as toys. Replace the sensory opportunity with cat-safe enrichment such as sturdy balls, cardboard scratchers, food puzzles, or supervised wand play.

If your cat likes manipulating objects, cardboard-box enrichment offers a safer outlet when the box is clean and free of staples, tape, and loose pieces. If the cat also seems unusually hungry, compare the pattern with increased appetite in cats rather than assuming every non-food behavior is boredom.

If You Think Your Cat Swallowed Plastic

Do not induce vomiting, give oils or laxatives, or pull visible string-like material unless a veterinarian specifically instructs you. Contact a veterinary professional for guidance, especially if a large, sharp, long, or unknown amount may have been swallowed.

Vomiting, repeated retching, reduced appetite, abdominal pain, lethargy, diarrhea, constipation, or inability to keep food down can occur with gastrointestinal obstruction. If appetite drops, loss of appetite in cats is an additional reason to seek timely advice.

What to Record Before the Vet Visit

Note what material the cat targets, whether it only licks or actually swallows it, when the behavior occurs, and whether there are appetite, weight, stool, vomiting, or activity changes. That pattern is more useful than trying to assign one cause from a single episode.

sources.title: Pica in Cats
Gastrointestinal Obstruction in Small Animals

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Stare at Me? Read the Eyes With the Rest of the Body
articles.metaDescription: Learn why cats stare at people, how slow blinking and body language change the meaning, and when a new staring habit may signal a health or vision problem.
articles.alt: Calm cat looking attentively at its owner from across a room
articles.summary: Interpret staring through body language, routine and context, understand what slow-blink research actually shows, and recognize changes that may need veterinary attention.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat stare at me
secondaryKeywords: why is my cat watching me
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
A cat can stare because it expects food, is tracking your movement, wants interaction, is monitoring a routine, or is simply resting while looking in your direction. The eyes alone rarely tell the whole story. Ears, tail, posture, distance, and what happens next are more informative.

Use the Whole Body to Read the Stare

More Relaxed ContextMore Tense Context
Loose postureBody frozen or crouched
Neutral earsEars flattened or sharply rotated
Can look away or groomCannot disengage from the trigger
Soft eyes or slow blinkingHard fixed attention with escalating tension
Loose tailTail lashing or thumping

Context matters because the same eye contact can occur during calm social interaction, food anticipation, play, fear, or conflict.

Slow Blinking Has Actual Research Behind It

A controlled study published in Scientific Reports found that cats showed more eye narrowing after humans used slow-blink signals, and cats were more likely to approach an unfamiliar experimenter after a slow-blink interaction than after a neutral expression. That supports slow blinking as a potentially positive part of cat–human communication, while not turning every blink into a guaranteed emotional message.

Staring Often Tracks Routines

If your cat watches you at the same time every morning and then walks toward the feeding area, the stare may belong to a learned sequence. If it happens when you reach for a toy, open a door, or sit in a favorite chair, your behavior may be predicting what comes next.

Avoid responding to every stare with food. If the cat seems hungry throughout the day, use the guide to persistent hunger in cats to separate learned food requests from a possible health change.

Staring Between Cats Can Be More Important

In multi-cat homes, one cat can create social pressure without an obvious fight. A fixed stare from a doorway, hallway, or resource area may cause another cat to hesitate before approaching food, water, a litter box, or a resting place. Spread key resources through the home so one cat cannot control access to all of them.

If a new cat recently arrived, do not force face-to-face contact. Follow a gradual process such as introducing two cats in stages.

Three Questions for a New Staring Habit

  1. Is it new? A longstanding relaxed habit is different from a sudden change.
  2. Can the cat disengage? A relaxed cat should be able to look away, move, groom, eat, or rest normally.
  3. Did anything else change? Appetite, vision, mobility, vocalization, sleep, and social behavior add important context.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Seek veterinary advice if a new staring pattern occurs with disorientation, bumping into objects, unusual pupil appearance, apparent vision loss, sudden aggression, weakness, seizures, or another major behavior change. The goal is not to diagnose illness from eye contact; it is to notice when familiar behavior becomes part of a larger change.

sources.title: The Role of Cat Eye Narrowing Movements in Cat–Human Communication
CATastrophic Myths Part 1: Common Misconceptions About the Social Behavior of Domestic Cats
sources.publisher: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery / PMC

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Run Around After Pooping? Normal Zoomies vs. Litter-Box Clues
articles.metaDescription: Learn when post-poop zoomies are harmless, which litter-box and stool clues matter more than the sprint, and when straining or elimination changes need veterinary care.
articles.alt: Playful cat running away from a clean litter box
articles.summary: Focus on stool quality, straining and litter-box behavior to tell a quirky post-poop sprint from a pattern that may reflect digestive or urinary discomfort.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat run around after pooping
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Some cats sprint out of the litter box immediately after defecating and race through the house. If the cat passes normal stool comfortably, uses the box normally, and settles soon afterward, the run may simply be an individual post-litter routine. The important clues are usually inside the box, not during the sprint.

Watch What Happens Before the Zoomies

A playful dash after a quick, comfortable bowel movement is very different from a cat that strains, cries, repeatedly enters and exits, or produces hard, loose, bloody, or mucus-coated stool. Those details tell you whether the behavior is likely harmless or connected to discomfort.

What You ObserveWhy It Matters
Normal stool, no straining, brief playful sprintMore consistent with a harmless routine.
Hard, dry stool and prolonged effortCan occur with constipation.
Repeated urgent trips or diarrheaMay reflect gastrointestinal irritation or urgency.
Crying, blood, obvious pain, or hiding afterwardNeeds veterinary attention.
Repeated squatting with little or no urineCan be a urinary emergency, not constipation.

The Litter-Box Setup Still Matters

A dirty box, cramped covered box, noisy location, or route that can be blocked by another pet may make a cat leave quickly. Keep the box clean and easy to enter and exit. In multi-cat homes, distribute litter boxes so that one animal cannot guard every route.

If your cat starts defecating outside the box rather than simply running afterward, use the separate guide on pooping outside the litter box while still urinating inside it.

Do Not Confuse Constipation With Urinary Straining

Owners can reasonably mistake repeated squatting for an attempt to pass stool. A cat that repeatedly strains in the litter box but produces little or no urine needs prompt veterinary attention, particularly if distressed. Urinary obstruction can become life-threatening.

Keep a Short Observation Log if the Pattern Is New

For several days, note stool consistency, time spent in the box, vocalization, number of trips, appetite, water intake, and whether the cat behaves normally afterward. A short video of the behavior can also help a veterinarian understand the sequence, as long as recording does not delay care when the cat appears distressed.

When Observation Is Reasonable

A longstanding pattern is more reassuring when stool remains normal, there is no prolonged straining, the cat eats and drinks normally, and the sprint is brief and playful. You do not need to stop harmless zoomies; make the route safer by moving fragile objects and improving traction on slippery floors if needed.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Arrange veterinary care for repeated straining, hard or infrequent stool, persistent diarrhea, blood, vomiting, abdominal pain, reduced appetite, weight loss, or a sudden major change in elimination. If your cat stops eating at the same time, loss of appetite deserves prompt attention.

sources.title: Disorders of the Stomach and Intestines in Cats
Feline Environmental Needs Guidelines

articles.title: Why Do Cats Love Boxes? Hiding, Play, and Safer Enrichment
articles.metaDescription: Learn why boxes appeal to cats, what research says about hiding and stress, how to use cardboard safely, and when sudden hiding behavior deserves attention.
articles.alt: Content cat sitting inside a clean cardboard box
articles.summary: Use clean cardboard boxes as optional hiding and play enrichment, reduce preventable hazards, and recognize when increased hiding may be part of illness or stress.
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Cardboard boxes work unusually well as cat enrichment because one simple object can provide hiding, resting, texture, scent, and play. Research in shelter and veterinary settings also supports the value of hiding opportunities for reducing stress in many cats.

Why a Box Can Feel Useful to a Cat

Enclosed spaces give a cat more control over how exposed it feels. The cat can watch the room from one opening, retreat from activity, or sleep with fewer directions to monitor. A box can also be scratched, rubbed against, explored, and used as cover during play.

Studies of shelter cats have found that access to a hiding box can reduce behavioral stress and help some cats adapt faster to a new environment. That does not mean every household cat needs to spend the day hidden; it means that having the option to hide can be valuable.

Use the Box as Choice, Not Confinement

Do not put a cat into a box and block the exit. Place it where the cat can enter and leave voluntarily. Shy cats may prefer a quiet location against a wall, while confident cats may use a box in the middle of household activity. Senior cats may benefit from a low entry.

A Better Box Safety Check

  • Remove staples, loose tape, ribbon, string, and plastic.
  • Discard damp, moldy, chemically contaminated, or heavily soiled boxes.
  • Cut openings smoothly so there are no sharp cardboard edges.
  • Keep at least one clear exit.
  • Do not stack boxes where they can collapse onto the cat.
  • Remove torn pieces if your cat begins swallowing cardboard.

Turn One Box Into Several Types of Enrichment

Try a plain hide one week and a play box the next. You can cut large paw holes, place a cat-safe toy inside, or move a wand toy around the outside during supervised play. Rotation can create novelty without filling the room with clutter.

For a newly adopted cat, a box is only one part of a good setup. Food, water, litter, resting places, scratching surfaces, and predictable human interaction all matter. See how to set up a new cat's first days at home. In a multi-cat household, use a gradual two-cat introduction rather than expecting one shared hiding place to prevent conflict.

Chewing the Box Is a Different Question

Shredding or mouthing cardboard during play can occur, but repeated ingestion of non-food material deserves more attention. If your cat also seeks plastic, use the guide to plastic licking and pica-like behavior.

When Hiding Becomes a Health Clue

A cat that has always enjoyed boxes is different from a social cat that suddenly spends most of the day hidden. Watch whether it still eats, drinks, uses the litter box, grooms, moves comfortably, and interacts as usual. Reduced appetite, weakness, abnormal breathing, vomiting, diarrhea, urinary changes, pain, or sudden mobility problems should lower the threshold for veterinary advice.

sources.title: The Effect of a Hiding Box on Stress Levels and Body Weight in Dutch Shelter Cats
2022 ISFM/AAFP Cat Friendly Veterinary Environment Guidelines
sources.publisher: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery / PMC

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Chirp at Birds? What Chattering Usually Means
articles.metaDescription: Learn why cats chirp or chatter at birds, how hunting arousal may contribute, how to use window watching safely, and when unusual vocalization needs veterinary attention.
articles.alt: Indoor cat watching birds safely through a closed window
articles.summary: Understand why cats chatter at birds, provide safer hunting-style enrichment, prevent outdoor and redirected-aggression risks, and recognize abnormal vocalization.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat chirp at birds
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Rapid chattering, clicking, or chirping at a bird outside the window is usually seen during intense visual focus. Veterinary behavior resources commonly describe it as a response to the excitement—and possibly frustration—of watching prey that the cat cannot reach.

What the Behavior Usually Looks Like

The cat may freeze at the window, track a bird with its eyes and head, flick the tail, and make short clicks or chirps while the jaw moves quickly. Some cats do this with insects, squirrels, or moving toys too. Others watch silently.

Why Birds Trigger Such Strong Attention

Cats are hunters, and fast, irregular movement can trigger stalking, chasing, pouncing, and capture-related behavior. Watching wildlife through a secure window provides visual stimulation without requiring the cat to actually hunt outdoors.

The exact reason for the vocalization itself is not fully established. It is safer to describe chattering as associated with arousal and predatory interest than to claim the cat is making one specific sound for one specific purpose.

When Window Watching Is Good Enrichment

If the cat watches, chirps, and then settles normally, there is usually no reason to interrupt. Provide a stable perch, secure screens, and enough space to move away from the window. Follow bird-watching with a short interactive play session if your cat remains energized.

Wand toys and other moving toys can provide a safer outlet for stalking and pouncing. Rotate toys and end sessions before the cat becomes exhausted or frustrated. The same need for object play can also show up in pawing and knocking household objects or carrying toys to people.

Do Not Use Wildlife as a Toy

Letting a cat roam outdoors specifically to satisfy hunting behavior creates risks to the cat and to wildlife. Indoor play, secure catios, enclosed outdoor areas, or other controlled access can provide stimulation with fewer hazards.

When the Arousal Spills Over

Most chirping is harmless, but some cats become intensely aroused by an outdoor animal and then swat or bite a nearby pet or person. If that happens, do not grab the cat. Increase distance, block the visual trigger temporarily, and allow time to settle. Repeated redirected aggression warrants veterinary or qualified behavior support.

When a New Vocalization Deserves Attention

Chattering at visible prey is different from unexplained jaw movements, drooling, gagging, coughing, breathing difficulty, oral pain, or vocalization that occurs without a trigger. If the behavior changes suddenly or appears with physical symptoms, record what you can safely observe and contact a veterinarian.

sources.title: 10 Weird Sounds Pets Make (and How to Interpret Them)
Cat Behavior and Training - Play and Play Toys
2019 Meeting the Physical and Emotional Needs of Owned Indoor Cats

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Scratch Around the Food Bowl? What the Pawing May Mean
articles.metaDescription: Learn why cats may scratch around a food bowl, how feeding setup and appetite change the interpretation, and when pawing plus poor intake needs veterinary care.
articles.alt: Cat gently pawing the floor beside a clean food bowl
articles.summary: Interpret food-bowl pawing in the context of actual intake, feeding setup and competition, and know when appetite changes are more important than the scratching itself.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat scratch around food bowl
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
When a cat scratches the floor beside a food bowl, the movement can look like an attempt to bury the meal. In many cats it is a harmless pawing routine, especially when appetite, body weight, and eating behavior are normal. The exact motive cannot be proven from the scraping motion alone.

Start With the Meal, Not the Pawing

Ask what happens before and after the scratching. Does the cat eat normally and scrape only after finishing? Does it paw around the bowl and walk away without eating? Does the behavior appear only around one food, one bowl, or when another pet is nearby? Those differences matter more than the motion itself.

Possible Explanations

A Covering-Like Routine

Some cats make repeated scraping motions around food even when there is nothing available to cover it. The behavior may resemble burying or covering, but it is better treated as an observed pattern than as proof that the cat is consciously “saving” the meal.

The Cat Is Finished

If the scratching happens after a normal meal, it may simply be part of how that cat ends the feeding sequence. There is usually no need to stop it.

The Feeding Setup Is Uncomfortable

Cats should be able to eat in a location where they feel safe. Competition with another pet, a noisy appliance, a narrow corner, or a bowl placed beside a litter box can make feeding less comfortable. Feline feeding guidelines recommend considering privacy, multiple feeding stations in multi-cat homes, and opportunities for normal foraging behavior.

The Cat Is Not Eating Well

Scratching followed by refusal to eat is more important than scratching alone. Dental pain, nausea, systemic illness, stress, or an unappealing food can all change intake. Do not assume a persistent appetite problem is merely “pickiness.”

What You Can Change Safely

  • Keep the feeding area clean and quiet.
  • Use measured portions so you can tell how much the cat actually eats.
  • Separate feeding locations when pets compete or stare at one another.
  • Use puzzle feeding or several small meals when appropriate for the individual cat.
  • Place an easy-to-clean mat under the bowl if the pawing damages the floor.
  • Avoid punishment; it does not explain or solve the feeding trigger.

When the Behavior Does Not Need Fixing

If the cat eats an appropriate amount, maintains a healthy weight, shows no pain, and the scratching is a stable habit, it may require nothing more than a washable mat. Changing several foods, bowls, and locations at once can make it harder to learn what actually matters.

When to Contact a Veterinarian

Seek veterinary advice for persistent reduced appetite, complete food refusal, weight loss, vomiting, drooling, difficulty chewing, bad breath with eating discomfort, diarrhea, lethargy, or a sudden major change in feeding behavior. If the cat is asking for food constantly instead, compare the pattern with persistent hunger in cats. If intake drops, see why loss of appetite can become important quickly.

sources.title: Feline Feeding Programs: Addressing Behavioral Needs to Improve Feline Health and Wellbeing
Feline Feeding Programs: Addressing behavioral needs to improve feline health and wellbeing
sources.publisher: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery / PubMed

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Sleep So Much? Normal Cat Sleep vs. Lethargy
articles.metaDescription: Learn how much cats normally sleep, how to tell ordinary rest from lethargy, which accompanying signs matter, and when a sudden sleep increase needs veterinary care.
articles.alt: Healthy adult cat sleeping comfortably on a soft bed
articles.summary: Compare your cat with its own normal sleep pattern, distinguish easy-to-wake rest from lethargy, and act on warning signs such as weakness or appetite loss.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat sleep so much
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
Cats normally spend much of the day resting. Many healthy adult cats sleep or doze for roughly 12–16 hours in a 24-hour period, but a fixed hour count is less useful than your cat's usual pattern. The more important distinction is whether your cat is simply sleepy or is becoming lethargic and less able or willing to do normal things.

Normal Sleep and Lethargy Are Not the Same

More Consistent With Normal RestMore Concerning
Wakes for food, play, or familiar soundsDifficult to rouse or uninterested in usual rewards
Moves normally after wakingWeak, reluctant, or unable to get up normally
Normal appetite and litter-box habitsReduced appetite, vomiting, urinary changes, or other symptoms
Longstanding sleep routineSudden major increase in sleeping or inactivity
Normal grooming and postureHunched, painful, disoriented, or unusually withdrawn

Why a Healthy Cat May Sleep More on Some Days

Age, recent activity, household schedule, temperature, and available stimulation can all change how much time a cat spends resting. Kittens may alternate intense play with long sleep periods. Senior cats may rest more, but new inactivity should not automatically be blamed on age.

Use Response to Normal Motivators as a Practical Check

A resting cat may still get up for a favorite meal, greet a familiar person, investigate a toy, or move to a preferred window. A lethargic cat may stay unusually still even when something that normally matters happens. This is not a diagnostic test, but it helps describe the change clearly.

Five Changes That Lower the Threshold for Veterinary Advice

  • Hard to wake or markedly less responsive.
  • Weakness, wobbliness, collapse, or inability to stand normally.
  • Reduced appetite or refusal to eat.
  • Breathing changes, pale gums, pain, or abnormal posture.
  • A sudden sleep increase together with vomiting, diarrhea, thirst, urination, weight, or behavior changes.

These signs matter because many illnesses can reduce energy. For example, anemia can cause lethargy and increased sleeping, but sleepiness alone cannot identify the cause.

What to Track for 24 Hours

If your cat is easy to wake, otherwise comfortable, and the change is mild, note appetite, water intake, urination, stool, walking, jumping, grooming, and interest in normal activities. Record when the change started and whether it followed unusual exertion, travel, stress, or a household disruption.

If sleeping is accompanied by reduced food intake, use the loss-of-appetite guide because cats should not go through prolonged periods of inadequate intake. If your cat also becomes unusually clingy or changes where it sleeps, sleeping on an owner should be interpreted in the context of the larger behavior change.

When It Is Urgent

Seek urgent or emergency veterinary care if your cat is difficult to wake, cannot stand or walk normally, collapses, has significant breathing difficulty, has blue or very pale gums, or appears severely ill. A cat that is simply enjoying a long nap should still be able to wake and interact normally when something important happens.

sources.title: Is Your Pet Sleeping Too Much?
Urgent Care for Lethargy
Anemia

articles.title: Why Does My Cat Bring Me Toys? Play, Hunting, and Learned Routines
articles.metaDescription: Learn why cats carry toys to people, how hunting-like play and learned routines may contribute, and how to respond without reinforcing disruptive nighttime behavior.
articles.alt: Cat carrying a small toy toward its owner in a living room
articles.summary: Understand toy carrying as play, hunting-like behavior or a learned social routine, respond safely, and avoid turning nighttime deliveries into a reinforced habit.
articles.primaryKeyword: why does my cat bring me toys
articles.author: Virixoo Editorial Team
articles.content:
When a cat carries a toy across the room and drops it near you, several ordinary behaviors can overlap: carrying a prey-like object, moving a valued toy, requesting play, or repeating a routine that reliably earns attention. It is usually harmless and can be used as an opportunity for structured play.

Look at What Happens After the Delivery

The next step often tells you more than the delivery itself. If the cat waits for you to throw the toy, it may have learned a fetch-like game. If it drops the toy and walks away, it may simply be relocating it. If it meows until you engage, social attention may be part of the reward.

Carrying Fits Normal Feline Play

Cats naturally stalk, chase, pounce on, capture, and carry moving objects. Veterinary behavior guidance recommends toys that allow those sequences in safe ways. A soft mouse, ball, or other cat-safe toy can become a substitute target for hunting-like play.

It Does Not Have to Mean “A Gift”

Calling the toy a gift is a human interpretation. The interaction can still be social and meaningful without pretending we know the cat's exact intention. A more useful description is that the cat has learned to bring an object into your shared space and may expect something to happen next.

How to Respond Without Creating a 3 A.M. Habit

  • Use the toy for a short play session when the timing works for you.
  • If you cannot play, acknowledge the cat calmly and offer play later.
  • Schedule active play before the period when your cat usually starts making requests.
  • Do not use hands or feet as prey.
  • Store string, ribbon, and wand toys after supervised play.

If deliveries happen mostly at night, shift more interactive play to the evening and avoid turning every nighttime arrival into a long game. If nighttime vocalization is also a problem, see why cats meow at night.

Make the Toy Collection Safer and More Interesting

Choose toys too large to swallow and inspect them for loose parts. Rotate a few options instead of leaving every toy out. Novelty can renew interest, and interactive play is often more engaging than a toy that never changes.

Cats that enjoy object manipulation may also push household items or explore boxes. Those behaviors are covered separately in why cats knock objects over and why boxes make useful enrichment.

When a Change Deserves Attention

Toy carrying itself is usually normal. Veterinary advice is more appropriate when a sudden change in play behavior appears with confusion, weakness, pain, appetite changes, abnormal vocalization, compulsive pacing, or another physical or behavioral change. The concern is the broader pattern, not the toy delivery alone.
